concepts.title: Why Sociology is a Science: Method and Objectivity

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Why Sociology is a Science: Method and Objectivity' refers to.
questions.a: Sociology earns the name of science less from laboratories than from method: systematic observation, comparison and evidence open to checking by others. Its object -- human beings who think and react -- makes controlled experiment hard, so objectivity means disciplined self-awareness about one's own biases rather than a value-free machine.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Why Sociology is a Science: Method and Objectivity'.
questions.a: Science is a discipline of evidence, not a place -- sociology studies people systematically while admitting the observer's presence.

concepts.title: Sources of Data: Primary and Secondary

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Sources of Data: Primary and Secondary' refers to.
questions.a: Social researchers draw on primary data collected first-hand from the field -- interviews, observation, questionnaires -- and secondary data already recorded by others -- censuses, official reports, newspapers, parish or panchayat records. Each source has strengths and blind spots, so studies often mix them.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Sources of Data: Primary and Secondary'.
questions.a: First-hand fieldwork or second-hand records -- know what each source can and cannot tell you.

concepts.title: The Survey, Sampling and the Questionnaire

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Survey, Sampling and the Questionnaire' refers to.
questions.a: A survey asks standardised questions of many respondents to map patterns across a population. Since interviewing everyone is impossible, researchers sample -- selecting a smaller set chosen so that it represents the whole -- and questionnaires or schedules collect the answers for quantitative analysis.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Survey, Sampling and the Questionnaire'.
questions.a: Ask the same questions of a well-chosen few and read the many -- that is the survey's craft.

concepts.title: Interview, Observation and Fieldwork in Anthropological Tradition

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Interview, Observation and Fieldwork in Anthropological Tradition' refers to.
questions.a: Qualitative methods probe meaning: interviews range from free conversation to guided discussions, letting respondents speak in their own terms; participant observation -- living among the people studied, as in classic village and slum studies -- records social life from inside. Fieldwork of this kind trades scale for depth and context.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Interview, Observation and Fieldwork in Anthropological Tradition'.
questions.a: Live among, listen to, and record -- qualitative methods capture what numbers leave out: meaning.
